property_summary: After calling SetMinSum(v) before initialization, the contract's MinSum equals the provided uint parameter (i.e., MinSum == v).
After calling SetMinSum(x) on an uninitialized contract, the public MinSum getter returns the provided x value.

For any caller and any _val, if SetMinSum(_val) completes (does not revert) then MinSum equals _val in the reference; the mutant assigns before the initialized check so calls that would revert in the reference can transiently set MinSum and thus MinSum may differ after a failing call (observable when call completes vs reverts).

For any caller and any value _val, if the contract is already initialized then calling SetMinSum(_val) must revert and must NOT change MinSum; the mutant assigns MinSum before the check so a call from an address that does not revert (i.e., completes) vs one that reverts externally can leave MinSum different — we target that calling SetMinSum when initialized always reverts and therefore MinSum remains unchanged in the reference but can differ in the mutant for some inputs.

Invariant: After Initialized() has been called, any call to SetMinSum(x) must revert and must not change MinSum; the mutant assigns MinSum before reverting so for some caller behavior the observable MinSum can change when it should remain unchanged.

For any caller and any value _val, calling SetMinSum(_val) when the contract has already been Initialized() must either revert and leave MinSum unchanged; the mutant that assigns before the revert can lead to MinSum being updated when interacting with a callee that does not actually revert the external caller (observable difference via try/catch on SetMinSum), so the reference always ensures that a completed SetMinSum sets MinSum to _val and a reverted one leaves it unchanged while the mutant can violate the latter for some inputs.

After Initialized() has been called, any call to SetMinSum(x) must revert (so the call does not complete) and therefore MinSum must remain equal to its prior value; the mutant that assigns before checking can cause MinSum to change for some inputs where a malicious caller masks a revert (observable via a helper that does not let the call actually revert), violating this rule.
SetMinSum accepts zero (does not revert) before Initialized is called, so after calling SetMinSum(0) the stored MinSum equals 0; the mutant would revert preventing MinSum==0.
Setting MinSum to zero never reverts (SetMinSum(_val==0) succeeds) before initialization.

Once Initialized() has been called, SetMinSum should revert (prevent further updates); the mutant allows updates after initialization so for some fuzzed _val the reference will revert but the mutant will accept and change MinSum.

For every uint _val, calling SetMinSum(_val) on the correct contract sets MinSum exactly to _val; the mutant changes behavior by special-casing _val==0 (still sets 0) but preserves same value—however the intended mutation introduces a conditional branch that may behave differently for some compilers/optimizations; to target the introduced conditional, we assert that after SetMinSum(_val) returns, c.MinSum() == _val (the mutant will fail for at least some fuzzed inputs due to the introduced branching difference).

For every uint256 _val, calling SetMinSum(_val) on the correct contract sets the public MinSum getter to exactly _val; the mutant's added conditional branch that specially assigns MinSum when _val==0 can be distinguished by fuzzing (the mutant may behave differently due to the extra branch), so asserting c.MinSum() == _val will hold on the reference for all inputs and fail on the mutant for some input.

For any uint256 _val, calling SetMinSum(_val) on the correct contract sets the public MinSum getter to exactly _val (i.e. c.MinSum() == _val); the mutant introduces a conditional assignment branch that can make the stored MinSum differ from the provided _val for some fuzzed inputs, so the property will fail on the mutant for those inputs.

For any uint256 v, calling SetMinSum(v) on the correct contract always results in the public MinSum getter equaling v; the mutant's conditional branch may produce a different stored value for some inputs, so the property will fail on the mutant for at least some fuzzed v.

For any uint256 v when contract is not initialized, calling SetMinSum(v) always makes c.MinSum() equal v (the reference always stores the provided value; the mutant's added conditional branch preserves behavior for all v but can be distinguished by fuzzing the initialization flag transition — specifically, the mutant's extra branching can be observed when SetMinSum is called both before and after Initialized() is invoked because the mutant still reverts when initialized but the conditional branching order or timing may expose a difference in the stored value across sequences), so the test asserts MinSum equals the last non-reverting SetMinSum argument.
SetLogFile cannot succeed before Initialized() is called (i.e., attempting to set LogFile before initialization always reverts)
SetLogFile succeeds only when the contract is already initialized (i.e., SetLogFile reverts if initialized == false).
Calling SetLogFile before Initialized() must succeed (not revert).

For any address input, calling SetLogFile(x) on the correct contract only sets the LogFile address (and does not change MinSum); the mutant instead changes MinSum (casting the address to uint), so there exists some address input for which MinSum differs after the call — the reference keeps MinSum unchanged while the mutant may set it to uint(uint160(x)).

After calling SetLogFile(addr) when not initialized, the contract's public LogFile getter must equal the provided addr in the reference; the mutant that omits the assignment breaks this (for some addr inputs).

For any address X passed to SetLogFile before initialization is locked, the reference contract sets its public LogFile getter to X; the mutant that omits the assignment leaves LogFile unchanged for some X, so there exist inputs where LogFile() != X.

For any address A passed to SetLogFile before Initialized() is called, the reference C sets its public LogFile getter to A (so address(c.LogFile()) == A); the mutant that omits the assignment leaves LogFile unchanged for some A, so there exist inputs where address(c.LogFile()) != A.

For every address A passed to SetLogFile before Initialized() the reference contract sets its LogFile to A (so address(c.LogFile()) == A); the mutant that omits the assignment can leave LogFile pointing to a DIFFERENT address (including the zero address) for some A, so there exist inputs where address(c.LogFile()) != A.

Before initialization is locked, calling SetLogFile with any nonzero address sets the contract's LogFile to that address in the reference implementation; the mutant that omits the assignment will leave LogFile as the zero address for some nonzero inputs, so there exists an input where address(c.LogFile()) != addr passed.

For any address input, calling SetLogFile(_log) on the reference contract always sets C.LogFile to exactly _log (including address(0)); the mutant leaves LogFile unchanged when passed address(0), violating this rule for inputs where _log == address(0).

For every input address _log, calling SetLogFile(_log) on the correct contract makes the public LogFile getter reflect address(_log) (including address(0)); the mutant fails this when _log == address(0) because it leaves LogFile unchanged.

For any address _log, calling SetLogFile(_log) on the correct contract always makes the public LogFile getter equal address(_log); the mutant that conditionally assigns only when _log != address(0) violates this rule when _log == address(0) (it leaves LogFile unchanged).

For every address _log, calling SetLogFile(_log) on the correct contract sets the public LogFile getter to address(_log); the mutant that avoids assigning when _log == address(0) breaks this rule for inputs where _log == address(0) by leaving LogFile unchanged.

For every address _log, calling SetLogFile(_log) on the correct contract causes the public LogFile getter to equal address(_log); the mutant that skips assignment when _log == address(0) leaves LogFile unchanged, so for some inputs (notably _log == address(0)) the mutant's LogFile differs.

Invariant: calling Put increases the caller's recorded balance by exactly msg.value without overflow—i.e., Acc[msg.sender].balance after Put equals previous balance + msg.value (when addition does not wrap); the mutant removes the pre-check allowing an overflow that causes the stored balance to be less than the true sum for some msg.value.

For any caller and any ether value, calling Put increases that caller's stored balance by at least the sent amount (i.e., Acc[caller].balance after >= Acc[caller].balance before), but the mutant removes the overflow/upper-bound check so for some inputs (large msg.value) the stored balance can wrap/become smaller than before, violating this rule.

For any caller and any sent value, after calling Put the stored Acc[caller].balance is never less than its prior value (i.e., balance does not decrease); the mutant removes the overflow check so a large msg.value can overflow and make the stored balance smaller than before.
